source_text:
Χριστοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν. εἰ δὲ τὸν νοῦν τοῦ θεοῦ οὐ καταλαμβάνουσιν ἄνθρωποι
γνῶναι, οὐκοῦν οὐδὲ τὸν ἡμῶν τῶν ἐχόντων νοῦν καὶ σοφίαν θεοῦ. 1 Kor 3,1–3 Οἱ
ἄπιστοι ταῖς θαυματουργίαις μᾶλλον ἕπονται· διὸ ὑμῖν λόγον εἶπον, οὐ μὴν τὴν
τελείαν σοφίαν τὴν ἀποκεκρυμμένην, τὴν περὶ τοῦ πάθους οἰκονομίαν ἣν τέλειοι
μόνοι πιστεύοντες καταδέχονται. 236 ἔτι τὴν περὶ τῶν ἠθικῶν διδασκαλίαν καὶ τὸ
διὰ τῶν σημείων πιστεῦσαι τροπικῶς γάλα καλεῖ, βρῶμα δὲ τὴν τῶν θείων
δογμάτων ἀπαγγελίαν. δύναται δὲ γάλα εἶναι καὶ τὰ ἐλαφρὰ παραγγέλματα, τὸ
τιμᾶν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα, καὶ οὐ μοιχεύσεις καὶ τὰ ὅμοια, καὶ δεῦρο ἀκολούθει
μοι. εἶτα εἰπών· σαρκικοί ἐστε, καὶ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον περιπατεῖτε, τοῦτο λέγει τὰ ἐν
ἀνθρώποις τιμᾶτε καὶ οὐ τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ζητεῖτε. 1 Kor 3,5Ἀντὶ τοῦ ἴσοι κατὰ τὴν
διακονίαν. 1 Kor 3,6–10 Τὰ μὲν ὡς ἐπὶ γεωργίας εἴρηται αὐτῷ, τὰ δὲ ὡς ἐπὶ
οἰκοδομῆς. αὐτὸς δὲ ἔφη πεφυτευκέναι καὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν δεδωκέναι καὶ θεμέλιον
καταβεβληκέναι θεοῦ. Παρεγγυᾷ τοῖς μετ' αὐτὸν οἰκοδομοῦσι τῷ θεμελίῳ, ὅπως μὴ
παρέργου τὴν οἰκοδομὴν ποιήσωνται. θεμέλιον δὲ λέγει τὴν πίστιν καὶ τὸ κήρυγμα.
1 Kor 3,11–15 Οὐ τῆς κτίσεως λέγεται θεμέλιος ὁ Χριστός, ὡς ψευδόμενοι οἱἈρειανοὶ
διϊσχυρίζονται, ἀλλὰ τῆς πίστεως· ἐκηρύχθη γὰρ ὁ Χριστός, καὶ πᾶσα ἡ οἰκοδομὴ ἐπὶ
τοῦτον γίνεται τὸν θεμέλιον. καὶ οἱ μὲν διδάσκοντες μίαν πίστιν κηρύττουσιν καὶ
τὸν εὐαγγελικὸν βίον καταγγέλλουσιν, ἡμῶν δέ ἐστιν ἑαυτοὺς ἢ λίθους ποιεῖν
τιμίους ἢ ξύλα ἢ χόρτον ἢ καλάμην. ὅταν οὖν εἴπῃ· ἕκαστος δὲ βλεπέτω πῶς
ἐποικοδομεῖ, οὐ κατὰ τὸν βίον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τί; θεμέλιον γὰρ ἄλλον οὐδεὶς δύναται
θεῖναι παρὰ τὸν κείμενον. ὁ διδάσκων τὸν Χριστὸν καταγγέλλει καὶ τὰ
παραγγέλματα αὐτοῦ δίδωσιν· λοιπόν ἐστιν ἀφομοιωθῆναι ἢ χρυσῷ διὰ τὴν
καθαρότητα, ἢ χόρτῳ διὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν. ἐὰν οὖν παραγγείλῃ ὅτι ἕκαστος βλεπέτω
καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, πρὸς τοὺς βουλομένους ἐπονομάζεσθαι ἀπὸ τῶν βαπτιζόντων ἢ
διδασκόντων. Εἴ τινος τὸ ἔργον μένει ὃ ἐπῳκοδόμησεν, ὁρᾷς ὅτι καλὸν οἰκοδομεῖ ὁ
οἰκοδομῶν· ἐκεῖνο δὲ οὐ μένει κατὰ μεταβολὴν ἐνίοτε χείρονος προαιρέσεως. εἴ
τινος τὸ ἔργον κατακαήσεται, ζημιωθήσεται, αὐτὸς δὲ σωθήσεται, οὕτως δὲ ὡς διὰ
πυρός. 237 ὑπερβατόν ἐστιν· οὕτως γὰρ ἀναγνωστέον· εἴ τινος τὸ ἔργον
κατακαήσεται, ζημιωθήσεται, οὕτως δὲ ὡς διὰ πυρός, ἀντὶ τοῦ οὕτως
κατακαυθήσεται καὶ ζημιωθήσεται ὡς διὰ πυρός, αὐτὸς μέντοι σωθήσεται· οὐ γὰρ
παρ' αὐτὸν γεγένηται ἡ ἐπὶ τὸ χεῖρον παρατροπή. Καθ' ὑπερβατὸν εἴρηται, ἵνα ᾖ
οὕτως· εἴ τινος τὸ ἔργον μένει, μισθὸν λήψεται, αὐτὸς δὲ σωθήσεται. εἴ τινος τὸ
ἔργον καυθήσεται, ζημιωθήσεται καὶ καυθήσεται ὡς διὰ πυρός. πῶς δὲ αὐτὸς
σωθήσεται, ἐὰν τὸ ἔργον αὐτοῦ κατακαῇ ὃ οἰκοδόμησεν; οὕτως δὲ ὡς διὰ πυρὸς
κρινομένου αὐτοῦ, μή τι παρέλιπε τῶν εἰς διόρθωσιν ἡκόντων ἢ ὑπόμνησιν τῶν
ἁμαρτανόντων κατὰ τὸνἸεζεκιήλ. 1 Kor 3,16–18 Πάλιν μεταβαίνει ἐπὶ τοὺς
θαρσοῦντας τῇ ἑαυτῶν σοφίᾳ. ὅτι δὲ ναοὺς μὲν τοῦ θεοῦ λέγει τοὺς πιστεύοντας,
φθείρειν δὲ τὸν ναὸν τοῦ θεοῦ λέγει. τοὺς λόγοις θαρσοῦντας, τὰ ἑξῆς δηλώσει. εἴ
τις δοκεῖ σοφὸς εἶναι ἐν ὑμῖν ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, γενέσθω μωρός. διὰ τί οὖν φθείρει
τὸν ναὸν ὁ θαρσῶν τῇ ἔξωθεν σοφίᾳ; εἰ θεοῦ ναὸς εἶ, ἐκεῖνον ὀφείλεις ἔχειν
διδάσκοντα καὶ ἀποκαλύπτοντα· εἰ δὲ ἀφεὶς τὸν ἐνοικοῦντα τῇ σῇ συνέσει κέχρησαι,
οὐκέτι ναὸν ποιεῖς τὸν ναὸν ἀλλὰ φθείρεις αὐτόν. εἴ τις δοκεῖ σοφὸς εἶναι ἐν ὑμῖν,
τοῖς πλησσομένοις καὶ βλαπτομένοις ὑπὸ τῆς ἔξωθεν παιδείας· διεστείλατο γὰρ
εἰπὼν ἐν ὑμῖν. Τοὺς κατηχθέντας καὶ δεξαμένους τὸν λόγον τῆς γνώσεως ἐν ἑαυτοῖς
καὶ μὴ παρασαλευθέντας καὶ τὴν διδαχήν, τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος ναοὺς ὀνομάζει καὶ
οἴκους ἀκινήτους τοῦ ἐνοικήσαντος πνεύματος· τοὺς δὲ πράξαντάς τι τῆς τοῦ
πνεύματος ἐνεργείας ἄξιον, τούτους πνευματικοὺς καλεῖ, ὥσπερ ῥητορικοὺς καὶ
τεχνικούς φαμεν τοὺς τῆς τέχνης καὶ τῆς ῥητορικῆς ποιησαμένους ἐπίδειξιν. οἱ οὖν
ἑτέραν διδασκαλίαν ἐκ τῆς ἔξωθεν σοφίας παραδεχόμενοι, οὗτοι ἔφθειραν ἑαυτῶν
τὸν λογισμὸν παραχαράττοντες τὴν πίστιν τὸν τοῦ πνεύματος ναόν. διὸ ἀπειλεῖ
τούτους ὑπὸ θεοῦ διαφθαρήσεσθαι, ὅτι καταλιπόντες τὸν ἐνοικοῦντα διδάσκαλον
περὶ τὴν ἔξω σοφίαν ἐπλανήθησαν ἱκανὴν οὖσαν πρὸς ἐφόδιον ἀπάτης. 238,ξολ2 ∆ι'
ὧν τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ κόσμου τούτου ἀπαγορεύει οὖσαν ἱκανὴν πρὸς ἀπάτην,
διεστείλατο τοὺς πληττομένους τῷ ἐλέγχῳ. 1 Kor 3,21–23 Παραγγείλας μὴ
προσδέχεσθαι τὴν ἔξω σοφίαν, διδάσκει μήτε ἐπὶ σοφοῖς ἀνθρώποις καυχᾶσθαι·
pass_a_gloss: (Continuing: we have the mind) of Christ our God. And if men do not grasp the mind of God to know (it), then neither (do they grasp) ours, who have the mind and wisdom of God. [Label 1 Cor 3:1-3.] The unbelievers follow rather the wonder-workings; therefore I spoke a word to you, not indeed the perfect wisdom, the hidden (one), the dispensation about the Passion, which only the perfect, believing, accept. [page 236] Further, he figuratively calls milk the teaching about morals and believing through the signs, and solid food the announcement of the divine doctrines. And milk can also be the light commands: to honour father and mother (Exod 20:12), and 'you shall not commit adultery' (Exod 20:14) and the like, and 'come, follow me' (Matt 19:21). Then saying 'you are fleshly and walk according to man', he says this: you honour the things among men and do not seek the things of God. [Label 1 Cor 3:5.] Instead of: equal according to the ministry. [Label 1 Cor 3:6-10.] Some things are said by him as about farming, others as about building. He said that he himself has planted and has given the beginning and has laid the foundation of God. He charges those building after him on the foundation, that they not make the building a side-work. He calls foundation the faith and the preaching. [Label 1 Cor 3:11-15.] Christ is not called foundation of the creation, as the Arians falsely insist, but of the faith; for Christ was preached, and the whole building comes about on this foundation. And those teaching preach one faith and announce the gospel life, but it is ours to make ourselves either precious stones or wood or hay or straw. So when he says 'but let each see how he builds on', (it is) not according to the life, but according to what? 'For another foundation no one can lay besides the one lying (there).' The one teaching announces Christ and gives his commands; it remains to be made like either gold through the purity, or hay through the weakness. So if he charges that 'each should see' and the following, (it is) toward those wishing to be named from those baptizing or teaching. 'If anyone's work remains which he built on': you see that the builder builds (something) good; but that does not remain, according to a change sometimes of the worse choice. 'If anyone's work will be burned down, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.' [page 237] It is a hyperbaton; for thus it must be read: 'if anyone's work will be burned down, it will suffer loss, yet so as through fire', instead of: so it will be burned down and suffer loss as through fire; 'he himself however will be saved': for the turning aside to the worse has not come about from him. It is said by hyperbaton, so that it is thus: 'if anyone's work remains, he will receive a reward, and he himself will be saved. If anyone's work will be burned, it will suffer loss and will be burned as through fire.' And how will he himself be saved, if his work which he built is burned down? 'Yet so as through fire', he being judged (as to) whether he left out anything of the things that come toward correction or reminding of those sinning, according to Ezekiel. [Label 1 Cor 3:16-18.] Again he passes on to those confident in their own wisdom. That he calls the believers temples of God, and says that those confident in words destroy the temple of God, the following will show: 'if anyone thinks he is wise among you in this age, let him become a fool'. Why then does the one confident in the outside wisdom destroy the temple? If you are God's temple, you ought to have him teaching and revealing; but if leaving the one dwelling (in you) you have used your own intelligence, you no longer make the temple a temple but you destroy it. 'If anyone thinks he is wise among you': to those struck and harmed by the outside education; for he made a distinction saying 'among you'. Those catechized and having received the word of knowledge in themselves and not shaken (from) the teaching, he names temples of the Holy Spirit and immovable houses of the Spirit who dwelt (in them); and those who did something worthy of the working of the Spirit, these he calls spiritual, as we call rhetorical and technical those who made a display of the craft and of rhetoric. So those accepting another teaching from the outside wisdom, these corrupted their own reasoning, counterfeiting the faith, the temple of the Spirit. Therefore he threatens that these will be destroyed by God, because leaving the indwelling Teacher they wandered about the outside wisdom, which is sufficient as provision for deceit. [Second column, page 238, parallel:] By which he forbids the wisdom of this world as being sufficient for deceit, he distinguished with the rebuke those who are struck. [Label 1 Cor 3:21-23.] Having charged (them) not to accept the outside wisdom, he teaches (them) not to boast over wise men either (… continues in the next section).
pass_b_english: …of Christ our God." If men cannot grasp the mind of God so as to know it, then they cannot know ours either, since we have the mind and wisdom of God.

On 1 Corinthians 3:1–3: Unbelievers are more ready to follow wonders. So I gave you a word, but not the perfect and hidden wisdom, the dispensation of the Passion, which only the mature among believers accept. He also uses "milk" as a figure for moral teaching and for coming to faith through signs, and "solid food" for the proclamation of divine doctrines. "Milk" can also mean the light commands: "Honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12), "You shall not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:14), and the like, and "Come, follow me" (Matthew 19:21). Then, when he says, "You are fleshly and walk in a merely human way," he means: you honor what is human and do not seek the things of God.
On 1 Corinthians 3:5: That is, equal in their service.

On 1 Corinthians 3:6–10: Some of this he says in terms of farming, some in terms of building. He says that he himself planted, made the beginning, and laid the foundation of God's building. He charges those who build on the foundation after him not to treat the building as a side task. By "foundation" he means the faith and the preaching.

On 1 Corinthians 3:11–15: Christ is not called the foundation of creation, as the Arians falsely insist, but of the faith. Christ was preached, and the whole building rises on this foundation. Those who teach preach one faith and proclaim the life of the gospel; it is up to us to make ourselves precious stones, or wood, hay or straw. So when he says, "Let each one take care how he builds on it," what can that refer to if not to how we live? "For no one can lay any other foundation than the one already laid." The teacher proclaims Christ and passes on his commands; the rest is to become like gold through purity, or like hay through weakness. So when he charges, "Let each one take care," and what follows, he is addressing those who wanted to be named after the men who baptized or taught them. "If anyone's work that he has built on it remains": you see that the builder builds something good. But sometimes it does not remain, because the will has changed for the worse. "If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire." The words are out of their natural order. It should be read: "If anyone's work is burned up, it will suffer loss, yet so as through fire," meaning that it will be burned up and suffer loss as through fire, "but he himself will be saved," for the turn for the worse did not happen through him.

This is said with the words out of their natural order, so that it runs: "If anyone's work remains, he will receive a reward, and he himself will be saved. If anyone's work is burned, it will suffer loss and be burned as through fire." But how will he himself be saved if the work he built is burned up? "Yet so as through fire": he will be judged on whether he left out anything that served to correct sinners or to warn them, as in Ezekiel.

On 1 Corinthians 3:16–18: He turns again to those who trust in their own wisdom. He calls believers temples of God, and he says that those who trust in eloquence destroy the temple of God, as the next words will show: "If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool." Why, then, does someone who trusts in outside wisdom destroy the temple? If you are God's temple, you ought to have him as your teacher and revealer. But if you leave the one who dwells in you and rely on your own intelligence, you no longer keep the temple a temple; you destroy it. "If anyone among you thinks he is wise" is aimed at those who are struck and harmed by outside learning, for by saying "among you" he marked them off.

Those who have been instructed, who have received the word of knowledge into themselves and have not been shaken from the teaching, he calls temples of the Holy Spirit and unshakable houses of the Spirit who has come to dwell in them. Those who have done something worthy of the Spirit's working he calls spiritual, just as we call people orators and craftsmen when they have given a display of their oratory and their craft. So those who take in a different teaching drawn from outside wisdom have ruined their own reasoning, debasing the faith, the Spirit's temple, like counterfeit coin. That is why he threatens that God will destroy them: they left the Teacher who dwells in them and wandered off after outside wisdom, which is well able to supply deceit.
On 1 Corinthians 3:21–23: Having charged them not to accept outside wisdom, he teaches them not to boast in wise men either…

lemmas.gloss: words out of their natural order (hyperbaton)

choices.term: Ἀντὶ τοῦ ἴσοι κατὰ τὴν διακονίαν
choices.english: That is, equal in their service.
choices.why: ἀντὶ τοῦ is the commentator's 'that is'; the old English 'Instead of being equal according to the ministry' (SOURCE_ISSUES item 17) reversed the sense.
rejected: Instead of being equal according to the ministry

choices.why: They construe the verse differently (the first joins 'yet so as through fire' to the burning of the work; the second joins 'he will be saved' to the work that remains and asks how the builder is saved). Two different notes, not a doublet.
Second-column form of the 3:18 remark (outside wisdom able to deceive; 'among you' marks off those struck by it); every sentence has a counterpart.

choices.term: οὐ κατὰ τὸν βίον, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τί;
choices.english: what can that refer to if not to how we live?
choices.why: Rhetorical question; English keeps its force.
Severianus' own words; translated as written, no label added by the translator.
